summary: This paper investigates how the choice of gold standard reference affects multilingual benchmark scores and model rankings. By holding system outputs fixed and exchanging the reference between delivered gold and expert reviewer gold, the authors demonstrate that scores can shift by up to 4.95 F1 points pooled (and 7.55 points in Hindi), sometimes reversing model rankings. They recommend that benchmarks retain annotation records and report a reference-sensitivity band alongside headline scores.

chk_setup.paper_excerpt:
Method

The design holds one thing fixed and varies exactly one other. The scored output stays constant; only
the reference against which it is scored changes. The unit of analysis is the prompt, the outputs are
the two annotator labellings, the references are the delivered gold and the reviewer gold, and the
metric is span F1 under two matching rules. All uncertainty is a paired prompt-level bootstrap, and
the ranking claim is tested as an interaction rather than as two separate verdicts. Figure 1 shows the
pipeline the references come from. The rest of this section defines each of those in turn: the setting
and matching rules, agreement between labellings, the reference substitution itself, and uncertainty.
3.1

Setting and matching rules

Every measurement is computed on the audited subset of Section 2.3, the only items on which all
four labellings coexist. A labelling assigns a set of spans, each a character start offset, an end offset,
and one type; duplicates collapse, and no span carries two types, so a start–end pair identifies at most
one span per set.
We score under two matching rules. Under S TRICT a span is the triple (start, end , type) and two
spans match only if all three parts are equal; under R ELAXED a span is the pair (start, end ) and type
is ignored. Both require exact boundary equality, so R ELAXED is type-agnostic exact-boundary F1
and the gap between the rules isolates the cost of type disagreement among spans whose boundaries
already agree. Neither credits a partial overlap, so we cannot decompose the remainder into boundary
drift and missed detections, and do not claim to. S TRICT is the standard rule for span extraction; we
report R ELAXED beside it so the type component can be read off directly.

Our design. We invert the usual arrangement: instead of varying the system and fixing the reference,
we hold the system output fixed and vary the reference, so any movement is attributable to reference
choice alone. The measurement needs a dataset in which the same items carry several independent,
equally defensible references. We use the annotation record of a production multilingual benchmark
for personally identifiable information (PII) extraction, covering six languages and 24,939 prompts. It
retains three things normally discarded: two independent annotator labellings of nearly every prompt,
the aggregate shipped as gold, and an independent expert re-annotation of a sample. The delivered
gold and the expert re-annotation are both defensible; a practitioner could have adopted either.
The two references are not interchangeable: the delivered gold reproduces one annotator’s span set
more often than the other’s in every one of the six languages, while the expert re-annotation has no
such preference, so the difference is structural rather than sampling noise (Section 4.1). Exchanging
the reference moves the score by 4.95 F1 points for one annotator’s output (95% CI [3.23, 6.27]) and
2.00 for the other (CI [0.26, 3.37]), with each output held fixed. Most consequentially, it changes the
comparison between two outputs: the paired interaction is +2.95 points, 95% CI [+1.97, +3.87], and
survives Holm correction over all 14 tests we report; the Hindi margin changes sign (Section 4.3).
The cause is not exotic. On 94.9% of audited prompts the shipped reference is identical to one of the
two annotator labellings, because an undocumented aggregation default usually kept Annotator A
when adjudication did not fire. The reference was therefore partly copied from the outputs being
compared. We report the resulting movement as a reference-sensitivity band and show how to
compute one from any retained annotation record.
We make three contributions. First, a procedure for measuring reference sensitivity that requires no
new annotation, only an annotation record that was retained rather than discarded. Second, evidence
that an aggregation default resolving ties by position is an evaluation bias rather than an annotation
detail: it is testable in two lines of code, and in this pipeline it put a measurable thumb on every
score the benchmark reported. Third, a measurement of what that bias costs on a six-language span
extraction benchmark, with bootstrap intervals throughout and the limits of the estimate stated.
A note on scope. The outputs we score are human annotation passes, not model predictions. The
object we audit, however, is the benchmark evaluation protocol: the same reference-construction
process determines the gold against which model outputs would be scored. Human passes are the
only outputs this record supports, so whether the magnitude of reference sensitivity transfers to model
outputs remains an empirical question. These are measurements of one annotation record, not a
general law, and a pipeline with a neutral aggregation rule would show less. That is the point: the
size of the effect is a property of the pipeline, and it is currently unreported.

Limitations

size of the effect depends on properties of that record, in particular an aggregation rule that favours
one annotator. We claim the method transfers, not the number. The reviewer sample is documented,
